entries.title: Nvidia forms national security committee after Huang affair
entries.summary: Nvidia has created a board-level committee for national security and export control. This follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, allegedly including one with a Chinese intelligence asset.
entries.content:
United States of America

Nvidia forms national security committee after Huang affair

November 17, 2026

Nvidia has created a board-level committee for national security and export control. This follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, allegedly including one with a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia on Tuesday said it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee. 

This follows the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China and working to help ensure higher quality chips crucial to AI development made it to the Chinese market. 

The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable company in the space of a month. 

What are Nvidia's plans for the new oversight committee?

Nvidia is calling the new group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.

Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair the committee, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).

The committee will meet at least once every quarter. It will also incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts.

Nvidia already has a lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team; these groups will report to the board-level committee.

"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Board Chair Harvey Jones said in a statement.

The company did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace, but the timing seemed conspicuous.

The decision was announced hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its still-stratospheric share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month. 

How has the scandal highlighted the question of US-China chip trade?

US President Donald Trump, whom Huang was influential in persuading to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other US companies and officials deemed prudent, welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday. 

"Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great company," he said during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with the other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea."

Trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell. He also owns shares in other big tech companies.

Huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to Nvidia employees. This followed widespread reports, seemingly based on US and other intelligence, that one of the affairs was with a woman who used to lead a Singapore-based cloud computing company.

That company, Megaspseed International, is a major Nvidia client and is suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls. Intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.

The reporting on the case also seems to show these suspicions had been known to US officials and other countries, including Singapore, for roughly a year.

entries.title: Iran dismisses report of alleged 'dirty bomb' attack on Washington
entries.summary: Iran has said CNN's claim that Tehran would attack Washington with a "dirty bomb" was an attempt to manufacture further legitimacy to continue the war. Trump has said his administration takes the claim "very seriously."
entries.content:
Iran

Iran dismisses report of alleged 'dirty bomb' attack on Washington

November 17, 2026

Iran has said CNN's claim that Tehran would attack Washington with a "dirty bomb" was an attempt to manufacture further legitimacy to continue the war. Trump has said his administration takes the claim "very seriously."

Iran on Tuesday dismissed a CNN report that Tehran was preparing a so-called "dirty bomb plot."

US President Donald Trump said his administration was taking the report "very seriously."

What did reports say about an Iranian attack on Washington?

Tehran's dismissal came after CNN reported on Tuesday that "Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC," citing multiple US intelligence sources.

The article also reported that "US intelligence has picked up Iranian chatter claiming that it has stashed bomb-making materials inside the country" and that "many national security officials assume that pre-positioned nuclear materials have already been in the US for years," citing, again, multiple US intelligence sources.

When asked about the story during his visit to the Philippines, Trump said that if there was such a threat, Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no other country has ever paid before."

"I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," he added.

Iran decries 'fabrication'

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei slammed the report, calling it "a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda."

"Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations," he said on X.

"Step by step, they are attempting to manufacture a veneer of legitimacy for further aggression and atrocities," he said, naming CNN's reporting on the alleged "dirty bomb plot" and The New York Times without specifying any of its reporting.

Baghaei also said the US and Israel hit water storage reservoirs "during the recent acts of aggression."

Where does the Iran war stand?

The Iran war, started by the US and Israeli strikes on February 28, continues as negotiations to bring an end to the fighting stall.

Both US and Israel have been holding off from major attacks as they held elections over the last weeks.

Tehran has said it is in control the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, while continuing to attack ships it considers unauthorized users of the waterway. There are near-daily reports of ships hitting mines in parts of the strait Tehran says are unauthorized for transit.

The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait.

Before the midterm elections, Trump said, "We may do another little Epic Fury," referring to US-Israeli strikes that started the war, though he did not provide any timeframe.

Trump is expected to meet Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of an APEC leaders' summit in China on Thursday and discuss ending the ​war in Iran.

Pakistan-mediated peace talks between the US and Iran on April failed to reach a conclusion.

Qatar, another mediator in the war, on Tuesday called for restraint "to avoid any escalation that could undermine negotiation efforts."

entries.title: APEC summit: What Trump, Xi and Putin want
entries.summary: Trump, Xi and Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of APEC. With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?
entries.content:
China

APEC summit: What Trump, Xi and Putin want

November 17, 2026

Trump, Xi and Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of APEC. With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?

The leaders of China, the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.

Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.

Several experts interviewed by DW do not expect any breakthroughs on US-China trade, technology or other issues. Maintaining the existing trade truce and preventing bilateral relations from deteriorating further may be the more realistic shared objectives.

Patricia M. Kim, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, believes neither leader is looking to significantly expand the bilateral agenda, as both have an incentive in maintaining the existing trade truce.

Over the next two years, Kim expects to see "neither uncontrolled escalation in tensions between the US and China nor a dramatic improvement in ties, but rather the continuation of the transactional détente we see today."

Zhang Lun, a professor at CY Cergy Paris University, believes Trump is under pressure both at home and abroad.

"Domestically, Trump faces the prospect of becoming a lame-duck president following the Republicans' heavy losses in the midterm elections," Zhang told DW.

"Internationally, damage to relations with allies, the weakening of the US-led international order, indifference toward democratic values and freedoms, and the difficulties encountered in the Iran war have all reduced America's leverage, resources and influence."

Zhang believes strained ties with US allies and the war in Iran have weakened Trump's hand with Beijing, making him more eager to secure diplomatic wins and Xi's cooperation on key policy priorities.

Contentious issues may be left for later

Jia Hui Tee, a senior trade policy analyst at the Hinrich Foundation, expects Trump and Xi to focus on stabilizing their fragile trade relationship.

She says the two leaders could make progress on reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion (€27.3 billion) on each side. "While the list of products has been announced, the timeline has not been set and an indicative implementation timeline would be an easy win" for both governments.

Washington wants Beijing to accelerate purchases of US agricultural products and increase exports of rare earths and other critical minerals. But Tee believes that "China would likely be cautious with delivering on its commitments especially when Trump is weaker at home after the midterms with Democrats pushing back on his tariffs."

She also points out that neither side would want to cede their bargaining chips easily, including rare earth exports and technology export controls.

With another meeting between the two leaders is expected in December at the G20 summit in Miami, "there is room to push more contentious issues to a later date and further extend the trade truce in the next meeting," Jia told DW.

China, the US and Russia: three leaders, three agendas

Russia hopes that talks with the leaders of the US and China will enhance its diplomatic standing and help secure a settlement to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow. 

Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, told DW that Moscow wants to create the impression that Washington is willing to sit down with Russia and negotiate. This, in turn, could undermine confidence in Europe and Ukraine.

"Trump wants trilateral nuclear talks," she said, while Beijing "wants the optics of China hosting the unprecedented historical meeting among the three."

Alicja Bachulska, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Beijing wants to use the meeting to demonstrate its ability to bring major powers together and facilitate international dialogue.

"Russia wants recognition, the US wants arms control, and China wants status without strings attached," she said. "I expect each leader to restate their own positions rather than produce real solutions."

Ukraine: why Beijing is reluctant to mediate

Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, told DW last month that China may be more concerned with the survival of Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime than with actively bringing the war in Ukraine to an end.

Russia remains an important source of energy and a key diplomatic partner for Beijing, Kimmage noted.

An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin." For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.

Zhang Lun believes the current situation is "most in line with Beijing's interests."

The Trump administration's pro-Putin stance has made it harder for Ukraine to resist Russia, Zhang said, while Europe has been forced to bear greater costs and has been weakened.

He argued that the United States has also "lost moral authority" and "the postwar international order and the alliances built around Washington have been further eroded," making China's "position and influence more prominent."

He believes Beijing wants to keep Russia from collapsing, but not support it so openly or extensively that it alienates Europe and other Western countries.

"At the same time, China does not want Ukraine to be defeated, because that would reduce Russia's dependence on Beijing," he told DW.

"For now, China is unlikely to intervene directly. Instead, it will wait for a more favorable moment and then potentially step in as a neutral mediator in order to maximize its gains."

Iran: little sign of substantive cooperation

W.A. Figueroa, an assistant professor of history and international relations at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, told DW that there is little indication of any real cooperation between China and the US on Iran.

The two countries do share some interests, "including opposition to a toll system in the Strait of Hormuz and opposition to nuclear proliferation," Figueroa noted, but "China has consistently called for negotiations and denounced both sanctions and military force as a way to achieve these or any other objectives."

Figueroa says China does not want further escalation or prolonged instability in the Middle East. However, Beijing has been able to manage the current situation without too much difficulty, leaving it with little pressure to change its position.

"China continues to provide Iran with crucial financial support through its purchases of Iranian oil," Figueroa noted, adding that Beijing's diplomatic support has so far brought no substantial change, largely because China has little leverage over either Iran or the US in the region.

entries.title: EU, ASEAN pursue deeper trade ties, but hurdles remain as businesses struggle with informal barriers
entries.summary: 2027 could be a landmark year for EU–Southeast Asia trade, with several deals nearing completion. But the harder task will be to ensure that businesses actually use them.
entries.content:
November 17, 2026

2027 could be a landmark year for EU–Southeast Asia trade, with several deals nearing completion. But the harder task will be to ensure that businesses actually use them.

The European Union and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) could be heading for a breakthrough year in 2027, when the two sides mark 50 years of diplomatic ties. 

A long-awaited trade agreement with Indonesia is expected to take effect, while a deal with the Philippines is nearing completion and negotiations with Thailand and Malaysia are making progress. By the end of next year, the EU could have trade deals in place with six Southeast Asian states, up from just two today.

The anniversary could also revive the long-standing ambition of a broader trade agreement between the EU and ASEAN.

On November 17, the European Commission hosted a dialogue in Brussels to discuss trade relations with Southeast Asia, including progress on existing and pending free trade agreements (FTAs).

But attention is turning to what comes next. "Finalizing FTAs is only the beginning, not the end," Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, told DW.

FTAs can reduce tariffs and remove trade restrictions, but that is of little use if businesses don't know how to use them, he added.

"Unfortunately, in many cases, this is where there is a failure. Communication and training are key," Humphrey said.

The hard work begins after signing

For Brussels, the priority should now be to tackle the less conspicuous obstacles to trade, he stressed.

Cutting customs delays, simplifying regulations, and helping smaller European businesses enter unfamiliar Southeast Asian markets will determine whether an FTA succeeds.

"European companies with little or no experience in Southeast Asia would benefit from greater on-the-ground support, particularly practical, firsthand guidance on informal business practices and the unwritten local rules," Alfred Gerstl, an associate professor at Palacky University Olomouc in the Czech Republic, told DW.

One option is to expand the assistance offered by European chambers of commerce, trade delegations, and EU offices in Southeast Asia. This could range from helping firms find distributors to explaining local licensing requirements and how to qualify for preferential tariffs.

In Vietnam, for instance, sustained pressure from Brussels has helped improve market access for European pharmaceutical firms. In Indonesia, the EU has worked on trade facilitation while pressing Jakarta over import restrictions and halal certification requirements, said Camille Nessel, a researcher at the Université Libre de Bruxelles.

Regular consultations with businesses on both sides could also help Brussels spot problems before they become trade disputes.

Trade policy has also acquired a geopolitical purpose in Brussels. "If trade policy is expected to reduce strategic dependencies, we are asking it to deliver on objectives that remain insufficiently defined, let alone demonstrating how to achieve them," Nessel told DW.

Diversifying trade and reducing dependencies

The EU wants to reduce its dependence on a handful of suppliers for the minerals needed for batteries and other clean technologies, while Southeast Asian producers, particularly Indonesia, want foreign investors to help develop domestic processing industries rather than merely buy raw materials.

The EU and Indonesia have already clashed over Jakarta's restrictions on nickel exports.

European investment in processing facilities, agreements on environmental standards, and greater regulatory certainty would give both sides concrete gains, said Nessel. "The real value of an FTA is not just opening a market but giving the EU the leverage to keep it open," she added.

Pasha Hsieh, Lee Kong Chian Professor of Law and Jean Monnet Chair at Singapore Management University, said Brussels should prioritize ratifying its investment protection agreements with Singapore and Vietnam.

Signed in 2018 and 2019, respectively, the agreements still require ratification by all EU member states before entering into force. "These delays underline the need to follow through on negotiated commitments," Hsieh said.

The issue is particularly relevant as the EU looks to develop investment protocols in other Southeast Asian states where investors have sometimes faced uncertainty over legal protections. Indonesia, for instance, has terminated numerous bilateral investment treaties, including agreements with the Netherlands and Spain.

Towards an EU-ASEAN trade agreement?

A larger question is whether the EU should continue pursuing bilateral deals with Southeast Asian countries or revive its original ambition of a region-to-region agreement with ASEAN.

The EU and ASEAN launched negotiations for a region-wide FTA in 2007 but suspended them two years later amid disagreements over wide economic disparities among ASEAN members and political concerns. Technical discussions resumed in 2017, but little has come of them.

ASEAN already has regional agreements with China and several other economies. Beijing upgraded its free trade agreement with ASEAN in October 2025.

Region-to-region frameworks extend beyond trade. Humphrey, of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, called for negotiations to begin on a region-to-region Digital Trade Agreement and Investment Protection Agreement.

The EU-Singapore Digital Trade Agreement, which entered into force in February 2026, offers a possible model for wider cooperation, he noted, adding that common approaches to customs procedures, supply-chain standards, and green technologies could create greater alignment with ASEAN members that are not yet ready for full FTAs.

"European businesses have long complained of operating at a disadvantage due to the lack of a region-to-region deal. It is high time that both sides elevated their ambitions and embraced the idea of working towards such an agreement," Humphrey said.

The 2027 anniversary would be a convenient deadline for agreeing on what comes next, but Gerstl warned against mistaking another round of diplomatic ceremony for progress.

"There is a risk that attention will focus almost exclusively on the 2027 summit in Singapore and that the group photo will become the defining image of the event, only for momentum to fade in the years that follow," he added.

entries.title: Guinea jails 200 in wildcat gold mining crackdown
entries.summary: A Conakry court has jailed 22 former local officials from the gold-rich northeastern Siguiri region, as well as 200 people accused of illegal mining. It's part of a wider crackdown that sent thousands fleeing into Mali.
entries.content:
Guinea

Guinea jails 200 in wildcat gold mining crackdown

November 17, 2026

A Conakry court has jailed 22 former local officials from the gold-rich northeastern Siguiri region, as well as 200 people accused of illegal mining. It's part of a wider crackdown that sent thousands fleeing into Mali.

Guinea on Tuesday jailed 22 former regional administrators and 202 others accused of illegal gold mining in the northeastern Siguiri region near the border to Mali. 

According to the UN Environment Program, unauthorized gold mining is a source of income for more than 300,000 people in Guinea. The country's rich gold mines pull in workers from across West Africa.

What happened in the gold mining trial in Conakry?

Conakry's Court for the Repression of Economic and Financial Offenses sentenced 22 former officials from Siguiri to two years each in prison for complicity in environmental degradation, destruction and water pollution. They were each fined 10 million Guinean francs (around €1,025 or $1,125).

The court also sentenced 202 alleged illegal miners — several of them foreign nationals — to three-year prison sentences. They faced the same charges plus an additional count of mining illegally.

They were ordered to pay a combined fine of 10 billion Guinean francs.

Beyond that, the foreign nationals were banned from Guinean territory for a period of 10 years.

Why is Guinea cracking down on illegal mining?

Guinea's government announced a bid to stamp out illegal gold mining earlier this month, saying it wanted to prevent damages to farmland and rivers and other environmental destruction.

These efforts turned violent last week as protesters and security forces clashed in the northeast, with 10 people killed and 13 injured.

More than 1,200 artisanal miners were arrested in Siguiri in November.

Many more fled across the border to nearby Mali, often then having to await transportation to their homes in Burkina Faso.

entries.title: US flexes climate action muscle at COP31 despite Trump no-show
entries.summary: The US government is snubbing UN climate talks in Turkey. That's prompted a delegation of American lawmakers, mayors and governors to make the trip instead, aiming to show climate action in the US is alive and well.
entries.content:
November 17, 2026

The US government is snubbing UN climate talks in Turkey. That's prompted a delegation of American lawmakers, mayors and governors to make the trip instead, aiming to show climate action in the US is alive and well.

The United States, isn't at the table at the UN climate conference in the Turkish coastal city of Antalya. It's the second consecutive year that President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly said he believes climate change is a hoax, has not sent a federal delegation to the annual summit.

But that doesn't mean the US is totally absent. Far from it, since more than 120 state and local leaders from across the country are attending as part of the "America Is All In" coalition.

"We understand the importance of showing up. And if others refuse to do so, we will," said Chris Wheat, executive director of the coalition.

It's crucial, he added, to show the world that "millions of Americans are continuing to press forward on climate action" — even if the message from Washington, D.C., is a different one.

Historically, the US has released more emissions than any other country, and it is currently the world's second-biggest emitter of planet-warming greenhouse gases after China. Since taking office in January 2025, Trump has actively promoted the use of oil, coal and gas, the fossil fuels that are heating the planet and contributing to an increase in extreme weather events. 

The president has also cut funds for clean energy projects and rolled back some of the climate policies of his predecessors, such as rules limiting power plant emissions.

Momentum beyond White House

The unofficial US delegation of mainly Democrat lawmakers, mayors, governors and ex-officials — including former Secretary of State John Kerry, former Vice President Al Gore and California Governor Gavin Newsom — are not taking part in the climate negotiations. But they have been holding discussions at events on the conference sidelines.

They are keen to send a message to the international community that, despite their government's absence, efforts to transition to clean energy are gathering pace at the state level.

Mike Williams, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, an independent liberal public policy research institute based in Washington D.C., said the presence of US lawmakers in Antalya sends an important signal that "there's quite a lot of us in the US that are still deeply invested in this. It's not just the person sitting in the White House."

Nearly half of US states, representing about 60% of the US economy, are committed to reducing emissions in line with the Paris Agreement — the 2015 global pact to limit global warming. Many have implemented initiatives such as tax incentives for renewables and other policies designed to curb emissions.

A report by America Is All In and the University of Maryland's Center for Global Sustainability found that current state policies, combined with market trends and falling technology costs, could slash US carbon emissions by up to 46% below 2005 levels by 2035.

States tout climate action

"Even if we find a hostile federal government, they're not going to be able to stop the momentum," Minnesota Governor and Kamala Harris' running mate during the 2024 presidential election Tim Walz told a crowd at the summit in Turkey, adding that his state was on track to have a "100% carbon free" grid by 2037, earlier than their target of 2040.

Walz said the state was also producing sustainable aviation fuel to reduce flight emissions, manufacturing green steel and increasing the share of electric vehicles. "It's all moving forward," he said. "So this false choice that we need to choose the economy over clean energy — that has been totally rejected."

New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham said her state — the second-largest oil and gas producer in the US — had significantly cut emissions from the potent greenhouse gas methane through stricter regulations. She also touted measures such as shutting down coal power plants and expanding wind and solar energy.

"The largest wind farm in North America is in New Mexico," she said. "We're going to show the federal government, I am undaunted by their lack of responsibility and effort in cleaning up fossil fuels."

What's next for US climate policy after midterms?

The climate conference comes shortly after the US midterm elections, in which Trump's Republicans suffered a significant defeat. Democrats in Antalya have been keen to reassure the international community that the US would return to the COP table in the event of a change of government in two years.

Jorge Gastelumendi, senior director of the Atlantic Council's Climate Resilience Center, noted that US credibility around climate change and foreign policy in general had been "badly damaged" under Trump. "And so it's going to be a matter of how that could be built back up."

Meanwhile, Governor Newsom of California, a state of around 40 million people that plans to get 100% of its energy from renewables by 2045, said the US administration's climate withdrawal was also hurting the country's competitiveness.

"We need to reengage in these international agreements, and we need to recognize that China is outpacing us in many critical areas," such as solar power and electric cars, he told reporters in Antalya. "There is no substitute for national leadership."

Williams from the Center for American Progress said he wouldn't hold it against any countries wary about the US returning to the climate negotiations after two exits under Trump.

"Nobody should be under any perception that the US would be welcomed back with open arms," he said. "I think there needs to be an effort to show a willingness to collaborate […] That's another reason why it's important we're here now to show that there is this very large undercurrent of support within the US in spite of what's happening."

entries.title: Students' List candidates take seats as Serbian parliament opens
entries.summary: Serbia's Student List's candidates have taken their oaths in the inaugural parliament session. As the new majority, they have 90 days to form a government.
entries.content:
Serbia

Students' List candidates take seats as Serbian parliament opens

November 17, 2026

Serbia's Student List's candidates have taken their oaths in the inaugural parliament session. As the new majority, they have 90 days to form a government.

Representatives of Serbia's student-led movement were sworn in as lawmakers on Tuesday, just over four weeks after they ended Serbia's strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic's 14 years of rule.

The Students' List candidates officially took their seats in the inaugural parliamentary session as the first step for the youth-backed party toward forming Serbia's new government.

The movement holds 140 seats in the 250-member parliament while Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) holds 103. The remaining seats belong to ethnic minority parties.

Hundreds gathered outside the parliament building in the capital Belgrade, to show their support for the student-backed lawmakers, most of whom are teachers, professors and other professionals with little or no political experience.

Meanwhile, SNS candidates were met with a negative reaction from the crowd. A woman in the crowd poured yogurt over an SNS member's head as she climbed the steps to the parliament entrance.

According to Serbian media, the newly elected lawmakers have been preparing for their first session for days. They will face veteran opposition politicians, including Aleksandar Vucic, who became the opposition leader after his defeat.

90 days to form a government

The Students' List will have 90 days to name a prime minister, present their programme and form a government, once the parliament is formed.

The movement unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focused on making changes in domestic politics and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with. 

They pledged to improve healthcare, boost education and double the defense budget, along with many other reforms.

The election of a new parliamentary speaker will also lead to the appointment of a new acting president. The speaker has held the role since Vucic resigned in September to run for prime minister.

A snap presidential election must be called by November 27 and held by December 27.

Both parties are expected to put forward presidential candidates, but Vucic cannot seek another term because the constitution limits presidents to two terms in office.

entries.title: Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future
entries.summary: Germany's fall from grace in recent years has seen the team drift away from the fans. But Monday's drubbing of the Netherlands and the impact of Jürgen Klopp, Florian Wirtz and emerging youngsters offers hope.
entries.content:
Germany

Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future

November 17, 2026

Germany's fall from grace in recent years has seen the team drift away from the fans. But Monday's drubbing of the Netherlands and the impact of Jürgen Klopp, Florian Wirtz and emerging youngsters offers hope.

"Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.

Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.

"Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.

"Instead, they'll be thinking: 'This could really turn into something. We have wonderful footballers, great characters," Klopp said, and added: "The lads are even surprising themselves."

The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach took the job in July after Julian Nagelsmann paid the price for another German early World Cup exit, this time to Paraguay in the last 32. Klopp always preached patience, particularly after his first two matches yielded a fortunate 1-1 draw with the Netherlands and a 1-0 home loss to Greece.

Klopp hallmarks starting to emerge

It paid off on Monday as Germany performed with the hallmarks of Klopp's great club sides — fierce pressing, intensity, pace and a measure of joy. Perhaps it is in Florian Wirtz that Klopp's impact is more notable.

The 23-year-old has struggled to make a significant impact at Liverpool since moving to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen at the beginning of last season. But he has four goals in his last four games for Germany and is demonstrating the ability that earned him a €125 million ($137.5 million) move to England.

"I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer," Klopp said after the Netherlands match.

"We've also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he's so vocal. He's the first pressing player, he can press two players without getting tired."

That quality was evident in Wirtz's first goal on Monday, when he won back possession on the edge of the Dutch box before combining some dazzling footwork with a brilliant, curled finish.

Scherhant, Gruda and Wirtz make their cases

But Wirtz wasn't the only attacking bright spot for Germany. Rookie wingers Derry Scherhant and Brajan Gruda both scored and were a huge threat throughout. Klopp gave debuts to both earlier this year as he sought to spread opportunities. The pair have offered Germany a pace they often lacked under Naglesmann and his predecessor Hansi Flick.

"They can both play, my goodness," said Klopp.

Scherhant, who opened the scoring with another stunning strike, spent many days of his boyhood on the terraces of the Olympiastadion in Berlin, where Monday's game was played. Unlike many pros, he bounced about Berlin's lower league clubs as a youth before Hertha Berlin signed him up. He then moved to Freiburg in 2025 and is rapidly emerging as a player who can implement Klopp's style and reflect the coach's attitude.

"A few years ago, people told me I wouldn't make it as a pro. Then I became a pro. And even then, some people still said it wasn't enough—that the Regionalliga (Germany's fourth tier) was the best I could hope for,” Scherhant said.

"It's just unbelievable that I get to stand here now with the satisfaction of having proven those people wrong."

Proving people wrong is also a major part of Klopp's remit. After failing to get beyond the quarterfinal of a major tournament since 2016, the German public's interest in and enthusiasm for its men's national team had waned. Klopp's mission he said, was to "to prove to Germany and the world that we can play soccer."

Germany need to change perceptions

While that was achieved on Monday, the loss (and subsequent 0-0 draw) against Greece in the Nations League game were evidence that it won't all be plain sailing. Indeed, Germany have had plenty of false dawns of late, as captain Joshua Kimmich alluded to.

"We've been through a tough time," he said. "A clear victory doesn't make all that go away," he added before saying that the task was to "turn potential into quality and a team that's all about 'what ifs' into a team that's all about 'reality.' That's the art of it."

Klopp too, for all his hype, was keen not to get too far ahead of himself.

"We want to gradually solidify it. We're not done yet. We still have a few areas to work on. But I'm looking forward to our future — it's crazy what's still to come," he said.

In Nations League terms, that will be a matchup with world champions Spain, or Portugal or Belgium before qualifying for Euro 2028 begins. For now though, Klopp and his players can enjoy some time with those smiles on their faces.

entries.title: Ukraine updates: Russia-Crimea bridge appears destroyed after strike
entries.summary: Zelenskyy said a strike on the Kerch bridge in Crimea was in response to continued Russian attacks targeting his country's infrastructure. Meanwhile, two bridges were hit in Russian attacks on Kyiv. DW has more.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine updates: Russia-Crimea bridge appears destroyed after strike

Published November 17, 2026last updated November 17, 2026

Zelenskyy said a strike on the Kerch bridge in Crimea was in response to continued Russian attacks targeting his country's infrastructure. Meanwhile, two bridges were hit in Russian attacks on Kyiv. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Ukraine strike hits Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea to the Russian mainland, stopping traffic

  • Images show part of the bridge destroyed

  • Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the strike on Kerch bridge an 'unprecedented operation'

  • Russia also struck two important bridges in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said

  • The attacks come as Ukrainian, European and US negotiators discuss future talks with Russia on ending the war

These are the main developments from Russia's war in Ukraine on November 17, 2026: 

Skip next section IN PICTURES: The Kerch bridge before and after Tuesday's strike

IN PICTURES: The Kerch bridge before and after Tuesday's strike

Skip next section WATCH: Could attacks on Ukraine's power grid trigger a nuclear disaster?

WATCH: Could attacks on Ukraine's power grid trigger a nuclear disaster?

European regulators warn that a nationwide blackout could create cooling problems at several Ukrainian reactors simultaneously. How realistic is that scenario, and how well prepared are the plants?

Skip next section Hungary suspends Ukraine rail traffic after Russian drone attack

Hungary suspends Ukraine rail traffic after Russian drone attack

Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar said that rail traffic was being suspended to and from Ukraine on Tuesday and Wednesday, after a Russian drone came down in Western Ukraine.

"A Russian drone recently crashed in Zakarpattia, ‌300 metres from the Mukachevo railway station. The ‌Hungarian ​crew of a train arriving from Hungary was ordered to disembark," Magyar said in a Facebook post.

"We are suspending rail traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for ​today and tomorrow," Magyar said.

Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban had earlier said that Russian drones had attacked Zakarpattia, targeting areas near Mukachevo and Uzhhorod, not far from the border area with Hungary.

"As Russia intensifies ‌its attacks on Ukraine's civilian population, similar operations against Zakarpattia, which until now has ​been relatively protected ⁠due to its geographical location, can also be expected in ⁠the future," ​she said.

Skip next section IN PICTURES: Kerch bridge strike

IN PICTURES: Kerch bridge strike

Skip next section Vladimir Putin briefed on Kerch bridge strike — Russian media

Vladimir Putin briefed on Kerch bridge strike — Russian media

Russia state media has reported that President Vladimir Putin has been briefed by Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin "on the situation around the Crimean Bridge," citing Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.

"Following the government commission meeting, Marat Khusnullin reported to President Putin on the situation surrounding the Crimean Bridge," Peskov told reporters.

"According to the Investigative Committee, on November 16 and 17, Ukrainian armed forces attacked the Crimean Bridge using unmanned aerial vehicle, resulting in damage to the structure," TASS reported.

Russian media also quoted Peskov as saying that the bridge linking occupied Crimea with mainland Russia would be "even better" after it was restored, giving an indication as to the extent of the damage caused.

"There is, of course, no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than before," Peskov said, quoted by Russian state media.

Skip next section Ukraine's Zelenskyy confirms strike on Kerch bridge

Ukraine's Zelenskyy confirms strike on Kerch bridge

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed that the Kerch bridge was targeted by Ukrainian forces, describing it as "an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure."

"Today, everyone can see the consequences for the main military crossing from Russian territory into our Ukrainian Crimea," Zelenskyy said in a lengthy post on social media platform X.

The Ukrainian leader said the strike was a culmination of an operation "carried out over several weeks" by his country's military and involved destroying air defense systems, radar systems and electronic warfare equipment in the lead up to the attack.

Zelenskyy said that the road section of the bridge was hit by "Palianytsia" drones and while the railway section was targeted by "Neptune" missiles and "Ruta" drones.

"We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection," Zelenskyy said and pointed to continued Russian strikes on Ukraine's infrastructure.

His post was accompanied by footage appearing to show the moment the bridge was struck and then the subsequent aftermath with one part of the bridge collapsed.

Skip next section Germany and Norway to purchase more air defenses for Ukraine

Germany and Norway to purchase more air defenses for Ukraine

Germany and Norway will fund a new US air defense package for Ukraine's defensive needs, according to Germany's defense chief.

"Russia is intensifying its air attacks because it is not making progress on the battlefield," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said at an EU meeting in Brussels.

Pistorius said that Germany would contribute $300 million (€272 million) towards the weapons package that would include Patriot interceptor missiles.

The package will also include previously announced IRIS-T systems, as well as new radars and ammunition for F-16 fighter jets and drones.

The announcement comes ahead of a meeting of Ukraine's military backers at NATO headquarters in Brussels later today.

Germany has, since the start of Russia's invasion, provided civilian aid totalling more than €45.7 billion and provided or earmarked military aid of around €57.8 billion, according to the German government.

Skip next section Power outages in 9 Ukrainian regions after Russian strikes — energy official

Power outages in 9 Ukrainian regions after Russian strikes — energy official

Ukraine's Deputy Energy ​Minister Artem Nekrasov, said that Russian strikes on energy infrastructure had caused power outages in nine Ukrainian regions.

"As a result of the strikes, some consumers have been left without electricity in the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Rivne, Sumy, Chernihiv and Chernivtsi regions," Nekrasov said.

"The situation is extremely difficult ⁠in ​the Dnipropetrovsk and ​Zaporizhzhia regions. Since ​last ‌week, Russia has been continuously ​attacking ⁠energy facilities in the ⁠Dnipro ​region," Nekrasov said.

Skip next section Russian government talks to be held after Kerch strike — Russian media

Russian government talks to be held after Kerch strike — Russian media

A government meeting is expected to take place soon following the strike on the Kerch bridge, Russian state media agency TASS reported.

"A meeting of the government commission on the aftermath of the attack on the Crimean Bridge, chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin, will be held soon at Government House," TASS quoted the Russian government as saying.

"The meeting will address issues related to the restoration of the Crimean Bridge and the organization of transport links," TASS reported.

The extent of the damage caused is not yet known and Russian officials have only confirmed that a strike had taken place and that traffic has been disrupted.

Skip next section Crimea strike kills 2, says Russia-installed governor

Crimea strike kills 2, says Russia-installed governor

A drone strike on Crimea has killed two people, according to the Russia-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov.

He said on Telegram that the strike took place in the Leninsky district of Crimea, which was seized and annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

Earlier Aksyonov said that Ukraine had struck the Kerch bridge, causing traffic to be suspended.

Moscow built the Kerch Bridge to link the annexed Crimean Peninsula to the Russian region of Krasnodar Krai in the northern Caucasus.

The route is a major source of supplies for Russian forces in Ukraine's occupied Kherson region and is a strategically significant target for Ukrainian forces.

Skip next section Kerch bridge partially destroyed, according to reports

Kerch bridge partially destroyed, according to reports

The Kerch bridge, which links the occupied Crimean peninsula to mainland Russia, has been partially destroyed, according to unofficial reports.

Photos on various Telegram channels appear to show that one of the arches and part of the roadway have collapsed following a strike.

Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski shared a picture on his X account showing a single arch where there should be two, simply exclaiming "Wow."

Reports on the extent of damage have yet to be confirmed by official sources, but images and videos of the bridge are being widely circulated in the Ukrainian media space.

Russia's Transport Ministry said there had been an overnight drone strike on November 17 leading to a temporary suspension of traffic. It advised motorists not to travel towards the bridge and wait for further information.

Skip next section Russian strike on aid distribution center earlier in the month killed 72, Ukrainian officials say

Russian strike on aid distribution center earlier in the month killed 72, Ukrainian officials say

Ukraine's national police said late Monday that the death toll from a Russian strike on a village in the southern Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia earlier this month had risen to 72.

Four people were still missing after authorities concluded a two-week search operation on Monday.

Russia hit a former school that was used as an aid distribution center in Komyshuvakha on November 2 as people were collecting humanitarian supplies. The attack was one of the deadliest of the war. 

The village is located close to the frontline.

Ukrainian police said Russia had attacked the search operation several times during the past two weeks.

"Unfortunately, the shelling of Komyshuvakha on November 2, 2026, became one of the most tragic attacks since the beginning of the full-scale war," Ukraine's national police said.

Skip next section Ukraine holds new talks with US, European negotiators

Ukraine holds new talks with US, European negotiators

Ukraine held fresh talks with US and European negotiators on ending the war with Russia on Monday evening, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian officials held online talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as well as representatives from Ukraine's European partners.

Kushner said progress had been made towards an agreement, although significant challenges remain to finding a path to peace.

The online talks come less than a week after delegations from the US, Ukraine and Russia met in Abu Dhabi for their first trilateral talks in nine months.

"Diplomatic processes are ​actively underway and we hope that these efforts will not be ​in ‌vain," Zelenskyy said. "Our team is working in the most constructive manner possible."

In his nightly video address, Zelenskyy also warned that Kyiv had intelligence that Russia would launch major strikes on targets across Ukraine on Monday evening and into Tuesday.

The Ukrainian leader warned that Russia "must know that for every act of evil they commit, there will be a just response from us."

In his remarks, Zelenskyy cited a Ukrainian intelligence report that said North Korea was supplying "dozens of ballistic missiles to Russia each month."

"This is extremely dangerous and not ​only for Ukraine," he said. "By ⁠using its ballistic missiles in this war, North Korea is making its weapons more effective. ⁠This creates additional challenges ​for the entire region around Korea."

Skip next section Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge for second day in a row, Russian authorities say

Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge for second day in a row, Russian authorities say

Ukraine struck a bridge connecting the annexed Crimean peninsula and the Russian mainland late Monday.

The same bridge over the Kerch Strait was also struck a day earlier, Russian-installed authorities said.

"At the moment, traffic is suspended," Crimea's Moscow-installed governor, Sergey Aksyonov said Tuesday.

Russian officials also said Ukraine had struck oil refineries on Monday.

Monday's attack was the largest such assault on Russia since it launched itsfull-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Russia says it intercepted over 1,300 Ukrainian drones during the attack.

Overnight into Tuesday, Ukraine targeted Moscow with nearly 200 drones.

Moscow mayor Sergey Sobyanin said early Tuesday morning that Russian air defenses had downed 20 drones heading towards the capital.

Skip next section Russia hits two major bridges in Kyiv: What we know

Russia hits two major bridges in Kyiv: What we know

Russia struck two bridges over the Dnipro River in Kyiv late Monday, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

"According to preliminary ‌information, ⁠there have ⁠been hits on the North and South bridges in the capital," Klitschko said on Telegram.

In a later post, Klitschko said the attack "caused damage to critical infrastructure," adding that there were "disruptions to water and heating supplies" because of strikes.

Earlier this month and in October, a series of Russian attacks hit several bridges in the Ukrainian capital, causing major disruption.

Earlier on Monday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned Russia was planning strikes for Monday night and into Tuesday.

"Tonight, overnight, and throughout tomorrow, please pay attention to missile danger alerts," he said.

"And they there, in Russia, must know that for every one of their evils there will be our just response," Zelenskyy added.

entries.title: Could the Airbus' €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?
entries.summary: The US says a record €3 billion financing package for Airbus may conflict with a transatlantic aircraft-subsidy truce. EU officials insist the funding complies with market-based rules.
